ideas.title: Calendar Sync Watch for WordPress Booking Sites

notes.stateful: Each booking page keeps a per-service baseline of how many slots it normally offers, a 90-day check history and an incident log the owner or freelancer comes back to.
notes.connected: Reads availability from each site's booking plugin (Amelia or Simply Schedule Appointments) and free/busy from the client's Google Calendar with the client's consent.
notes.unattended: A daily scheduled check per page, with an email alert on a failure and a weekly all-clear digest.
notes.engine: Per-plugin adapters plus the cross-check rules: no slots in the next 7 days against a learned baseline, slots offered inside the owner's busy times (sync dead), calendar quiet while bookings continue, with time-zone and opening-hours handling.
notes.shared: The freelancer watches many client sites from one account and sends each client a monthly health note.

buildPlan.title: One page, one check
buildPlan.delivers: Sign in, paste an Amelia booking page and a service, and see today's count of bookable slots in the next 7 days; a daily job emails if it is zero.
buildPlan.acceptance: Against a test WordPress site with Amelia Lite, the check reports the right slot count, and an alert email arrives after all working hours are removed; deployed.

buildPlan.title: Second plugin and sync status
buildPlan.delivers: Add Simply Schedule Appointments (public availability route with the page's public nonce) and read each plugin's own Google Calendar connection status where it exposes one.
buildPlan.acceptance: Fixture sites for both plugins return slot counts that match what the booking page shows on the same day; a revoked Google Calendar link on the fixture raises a 'calendar disconnected' alert, not a false 'no slots'.

buildPlan.title: Calendar cross-check
buildPlan.delivers: The client connects Google Calendar with free/busy access only; the check flags slots offered while the owner's calendar is busy, which means the sync is dead.
buildPlan.acceptance: A seeded busy block that the booking tool still offers produces exactly one 'sync looks broken' alert; event titles and attendees are never requested or stored.

buildPlan.title: Baselines and quiet alerts
buildPlan.delivers: A per-service baseline so 'only 2 slots this week' alerts when the norm is 30, with snooze for holidays and a weekly all-clear digest.
buildPlan.acceptance: Replaying 60 days of recorded counts produces alerts only on the seeded drops; a snoozed week sends nothing.

buildPlan.title: Freelancer view
buildPlan.delivers: One account watches many client pages, with a status board and a plain monthly health note emailed to each business owner.
buildPlan.acceptance: A 20-page fixture renders the board under one second; each owner receives only their own note.

buildPlan.title: Polish
buildPlan.delivers: Business-owner README in plain words, phone layout, keyboard and screen-reader pass, privacy notice on what is read, walkthrough test.
buildPlan.acceptance: A walkthrough test runs sign-in to first alert; axe reports no serious issues; the privacy page lists every scope and field read.

ideas.summary: For freelancers and small agencies who run WordPress booking sites for salons, clinics and studios: a daily check that each site's Google Calendar link is still alive and that each service still offers its usual number of slots, with an email before the client's customers notice.

public.summary: Checks every day that your clients' booking pages still offer times and that their calendars are still in sync, and emails you before their customers notice.
public.problem: You look after booking sites for salons, clinics and studios, and an update or a lapsed calendar link can quietly stop a page offering times. You hear about it from the client, after their customers could not book or two people turned up for the same slot. Checking every client's page every morning is a job nobody has time for.
public.forWhom: Freelancers and small agencies who build and look after online booking pages for appointment businesses.
benefits: Know every client's booking page is open for business without checking it yourself
Hear about a broken calendar link before it causes a double booking
One board for all your clients' booking pages
A short monthly note you can send each client to show their bookings are being watched

ideas.problemStatement: Booking plugins break quietly after updates: an Amelia update left an escape-room owner's 'free slots ... not appearing on the website', a security-plugin update 'prevented appointment bookings', and a paid booking tool's calendar 'was regularly disconnected, which meant that bookings were no longer possible'. Simply Schedule Appointments detects a dead Google Calendar link but only shows a wp-admin banner; its email alert is commented out in the plugin code. Whoever maintains the site usually hears from the client, after customers could not book.
ideas.description: The freelancer adds each client's booking page and picks the services to watch. Once a day a small backend reads the availability the page offers for the next 7 days through the route the plugin's own booking form uses (Amelia and Simply Schedule Appointments expose this to logged-out visitors), compares it with a learned per-service baseline, and, with free/busy-only access to the client's Google Calendar, flags slots offered inside busy times, which is what a dead calendar sync looks like. It emails the freelancer when something is off, with a weekly all-clear, and can send the client a short monthly health note. It does not try to catch front-end breakage (firewall rules, caching, script errors): the setup page links a free browser check for that. It places no test bookings, which keeps it apart from the existing Delivery Canary for digital shops.
ideas.targetCustomer: Freelancers and small agencies who maintain 5 to 40 WordPress sites with Amelia or Simply Schedule Appointments for appointment businesses (salons, spas, clinics, therapists, tutors, escape rooms), usually inside a monthly care plan.
ideas.buyer: The freelancer or small agency, from its own card, folded into the monthly care plan it already sells the client.
ideas.whyNow: Booking plugins ship often (Amelia 2.4.15 updated 2026-11-16, Simply Schedule Appointments 2026-11-17, per the plugin API https://api.wordpress.org/plugins/info/1.2/?action=plugin_information&request[slug]=ameliabooking&request[fields][sections]=0), and 2026 support threads show updates breaking slots and calendar sync (https://wordpress.org/support/topic/google-calendar-event-description-2/). Freelancers already pay about EUR 2 per site per month for generic monitoring that cannot see either (https://wp-umbrella.com/pricing/).
ideas.founderFit: Pisan can ship a web app alone in days on the HintWise platform, which already has sign-in, per-app data, scheduled jobs, transactional email and a small backend; the work is adapters and rules, which suits a CS professor. He has no stated salon or agency network, so reach relies on the WordPress plugin directory and freelancer channels.

mvpScope.buildEstimate: 3 weeks (6 build days of milestones plus Google OAuth verification lead time)

ideas.techStack: Static front end on the HintWise platform, Supabase sign-in and per-app tables (pages, services, checks, baselines, incidents), a scheduled job calling a small Node backend on Render that holds the adapters and OAuth tokens, Google Calendar API freeBusy, transactional email. No LLM needed.

pricing.model: Per freelancer account, by number of watched client sites
pricing.pricePoint: Free for 1 site; $19/month for up to 10 sites; $39/month for up to 40
pricing.rationale: Freelancers pay about EUR 2 per site per month for WP Umbrella's generic monitoring (https://wp-umbrella.com/pricing/); a booking-specific check is worth a small premium on that, and stays under Checkly Starter ($24/month) for a typical portfolio.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 80 freelancers or agencies at an average of $25/month = about $2,000 MRR after a year, assuming the free one-site tier converts through a WordPress directory listing; unproven, since nobody was found paying for booking-specific monitoring.
ideas.distribution: A free companion plugin in the WordPress plugin directory (guideline 6 permits plugins that connect to a paid service; trialware is not permitted, so the free plugin must work on its own, for example a one-page daily check) aimed at Amelia and Simply Schedule Appointments sites, which have 90,000 and 50,000 active installs. The wordpress.org support forums forbid promoting your own plugins or services, so no posting there. Second channel: freelancers and small agencies who maintain booking sites, reached through the plugin listing and through agency care-plan communities whose self-promotion rules were not checked this run.

validationTest.method: Interview 5 freelancers who maintain salon or clinic booking sites on Amelia or Simply Schedule Appointments about how they find out bookings broke, and offer a free one-time slot and calendar-sync report for their client sites; communities' self-promotion rules checked first, and not the wordpress.org support forums.
validationTest.successCriteria: 3 of 5 freelancers report a silent booking or sync failure in the last year, and 3 agree to a $19/month pilot for 10 sites.
validationTest.cost: About 4 days of work and under $50.

ideas.moat: Thin: per-plugin adapters and per-site baseline history are the asset. The plugin vendors could turn on their own disconnection emails, as Calendly already has; the cross-site board and client notes are what one vendor will not build.
compliance: Google OAuth: Calendar scopes, including calendar.events.readonly, are sensitive and need Google verification (no security assessment); request free/busy only to keep the data minimal and expect weeks of review lead time.

Health and personal data: clinic calendars can hold patient names (GDPR special-category data in the EU, PHI under HIPAA in the US); reading free/busy only and never event titles or attendees keeps the product out of that data.
Site owner consent: read only pages the customer owns or manages, respect Simply Schedule Appointments' rate limit, check once a day.
Plugin terms: read only the public availability routes the booking forms already use, on sites the freelancer manages with the client's consent; no plugin licence keys stored.
Accessibility: dashboard and emails to WCAG 2.2 AA.

risks.risk: Plugin updates change the internal booking routes the adapters rely on (Amelia's documented API is Elite-only and key-protected; the logged-out route is undocumented).
risks.mitigation: Pin adapter tests to each plugin's latest release from the WordPress API, run them daily on fixture sites, and fall back to a headless-browser read when a route changes.

risks.risk: False alarms from holidays, fully booked weeks or staff leave annoy owners.
risks.mitigation: Learned baselines, a 'fully booked' versus 'no hours' distinction where the tool exposes it, and one-click snooze.

risks.risk: Google verification delays launch.
risks.mitigation: Ship slot checks first; add the calendar cross-check after verification, testing with up to 100 users meanwhile.

risks.risk: Too close to the Delivery Canary idea.
risks.mitigation: Keep it to appointment availability and calendar sync, with no test orders or email-delivery checks in the first release.

risks.risk: Free browser checks (Checkly, OnlineOrNot) catch front-end breakage this product cannot see, so a freelancer may see it as redundant.
risks.mitigation: Sell only what a browser check cannot do (calendar sync, slot baselines, client notes) and link a free browser check in setup rather than competing with it.

risks.risk: A firewall plugin blocks the daily read from a datacenter address, giving false alarms.
risks.mitigation: Detect blocked responses separately from 'no slots', and document an allowlist entry for the client site.

scoreRationale.pain: Only two complaints fit the scope, both owner-noticed Amelia cases from May-June 2026 (https://wordpress.org/support/topic/version-5-4-9-all-in-one-security-aios-causes-conflict-with-amelia-plugin/, https://wordpress.org/support/topic/google-calendar-event-description-2/); the headline Calendly case was not silent because Calendly emailed the owners, and it involved Exchange, which is out of scope (https://community.calendly.com/how-do-i-40/sudden-exchange-calendar-disconnection-ionos-hosted-exchange-ews-anyone-else-experiencing-this-6143).
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: One dated paid job is confirmed, but it is a USD 40 fix after a Booknetic update, not a payment for monitoring (https://www.freelancer.com/api/projects/0.1/projects/?seo_urls[]=php/Fix-Booknetic-Booking-Error-after&full_description=true); freelancers do pay about EUR 1.99 per site per month for generic monitoring (https://wp-umbrella.com/pricing/); no evidence found that salon or clinic owners pay a monthly fee for a monitor.
scoreRationale.reachability: Self-serve via the WordPress plugin directory, which allows SaaS-connected plugins (https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/wordpress-org/detailed-plugin-guidelines/), into Amelia's 90,000 installs (https://api.wordpress.org/plugins/info/1.2/?action=plugin_information&request[slug]=ameliabooking&request[fields][sections]=0); the support forums ban self-promotion (https://wordpress.org/support/guidelines/) and Pisan has no stated agency network.
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Checkly Hobby gives 1,000 Playwright runs a month for $0, enough for a daily check on about 30 sites, and a browser check also catches front-end breakage that a server-side route read misses (https://www.checklyhq.com/pricing/); OnlineOrNot gives the same 1,000 runs free (https://onlineornot.com/pricing); Calendly emails on calendar disconnection itself; the real gap left is the calendar-sync check for WordPress plugins.
scoreRationale.feasibility: Kept at 3: Amelia's logged-out wpamelia_api /slots route exists (https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin/ameliabooking.2.4.15.zip). But it is undocumented, a request from a datacenter IP can be blocked by a firewall plugin, and a server-side read would not have caught the AIOS POST-filter or JS failures cited as evidence (https://wordpress.org/support/topic/version-5-4-9-all-in-one-security-aios-causes-conflict-with-amelia-plugin/).
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Kept at 4: Google sensitive-scope verification needs domain and brand verification, a privacy policy on the same domain, a demo video and a reason for each scope, and 'can take up to 10 days' (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/sensitive-scope-verification); narrow calendar.freebusy and calendar.events.freebusy scopes exist (https://developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/auth), but their sensitivity is unconfirmed.

review.findings: I re-read the key evidence. The strongest recent item, the Calendly Exchange outage, was not silent: Calendly emailed every affected owner, and the calendar type is out of scope. The two Freelancer spend items are a Booknetic fix job and a rental UX feature request, not monitoring spend. Only two in-scope complaints remain, both Amelia cases from May-June 2026, so pain drops from 4 to 3. For a technical freelancer, Checkly Hobby and OnlineOrNot Hobby each give 1,000 free browser runs a month, enough for a daily scripted check on about 30 client sites. A browser check also catches the front-end breakage (firewall POST filters, caching, JS errors) that an unauthenticated server-side slot read cannot see, so competitiveGap drops from 3 to 2. The plugin source shows a real gap on calendar sync: Simply Schedule Appointments detects a dead Google Calendar token and shows only a wp-admin banner, because its admin email is commented out 'until we have a better way to detect false positives'. I found no Amelia doc for a disconnect email, and none for Acuity. Google sensitive-scope verification is moderate work (domain and brand verification, privacy policy, demo video, up to 10 days) and narrow free/busy scopes exist, so complianceBurden stays 4. I found no evidence that salon or clinic owners pay a monthly fee for any monitor; the only per-site monitoring spend is freelancers paying about EUR 2 per site for generic tools like WP Umbrella. The $9 single-owner tier is unproven, and the $29 freelancer bundle is the only buyer with precedent. Total goes from 20 to 18. Re-scoped on review to calendar-sync and slot-count health for WordPress booking plugins, sold to freelancers and agencies; Calendly and the single-owner tier dropped; misread evidence (the Calendly outage, a rental feature job, the n8n reminders case, a Bookly bug) removed.

missing: pain 3 is below 4 (only two in-scope complaints, both May-June 2026, after review)
no evidence item dated within 90 days
gateGap.closedBy: The freelancer interviews in validationTest: three reports of silent booking or calendar-sync failures in the last year would lift pain to 4 and add recent evidence, and three $19/month pilots would lift willingnessToPay to 4, taking the total to 20 or more.

ideas.title: Class Pack Ledger for Square Studios

notes.stateful: The studio keeps a running ledger of every customer's packs, credits used, extensions and expiries, and comes back to it at every class.
notes.connected: Connects to the studio's Square account (OAuth) to pick up pack sales from Orders and customers from the Customer Directory; exports a monthly journal CSV for Xero or QuickBooks.
notes.unattended: A nightly job expires packs, emails customers 30 and 7 days before unused credits lapse, and freezes a month-end liability snapshot.
notes.engine: Credit ledger rules: oldest-expiring pack used first, class-type eligibility, freezes and extensions, per-credit value for deferred revenue, and a breakage policy applied at expiry.
notes.shared: The owner runs the door check-in, each customer gets a balance page by link, and the bookkeeper gets a read-only month-end export.

buildPlan.title: One pack, one check-in
buildPlan.delivers: Sign in, add a customer, sell them a 10-class pack by hand, check them in at the door and see 9 left.
buildPlan.acceptance: A signed-in owner records a pack and a check-in; the balance reads 9 after sign-out and sign-in; deployed.

buildPlan.title: Square connection
buildPlan.delivers: Connect Square; mark which catalog items are packs (10+1, 20+2); new Square orders for those items credit the right customer automatically.
buildPlan.acceptance: In the Square sandbox, a paid order for a mapped item creates one pack with the right credit count within a minute; a refund reverses it.

buildPlan.title: Door check-in and rules
buildPlan.delivers: A phone-sized check-in screen with name search and a per-customer QR code; class-type eligibility; oldest-expiring pack used first; freeze and extend.
buildPlan.acceptance: Seeded test cases (two overlapping packs, an ineligible class, a frozen pack) all deduct from the expected pack.

buildPlan.title: Expiry and reminders
buildPlan.delivers: Nightly expiry sweep and reminder emails to customers 30 and 7 days before credits lapse; customer balance page by private link.
buildPlan.acceptance: A pack seeded to expire in 7 days produces exactly one reminder email; the expired pack shows zero usable credits the next day.

buildPlan.title: Credits owed and bookkeeper export
buildPlan.delivers: Month-end report: packs sold, credits used, unused credits still owed, breakage at expiry; the Xero and QuickBooks journal CSVs and read-only bookkeeper invite ship only if the validation test found a bookkeeper who wants them.
buildPlan.acceptance: For a hand-worked sample month, outstanding liability and recognized revenue match to the cent and the CSV imports into a Xero demo company as a manual journal.

buildPlan.title: Polish
buildPlan.delivers: Studio-owner README, phone layout for the door, keyboard and screen-reader pass, walkthrough test.
buildPlan.acceptance: A walkthrough test runs connect-Square to month-end export; axe reports no serious issues.

ideas.summary: For small yoga, dance and fitness studios that sell class packs as ordinary Square items: a credit ledger fed by Square sales, door check-in, expiry reminders and a month-end figure for unused classes, as a cheap add-on rather than a new studio platform.

public.summary: Keeps track of every student's class pack, checks them in at the door, reminds them before credits run out, and gives your bookkeeper a clean month-end figure for unused classes.
public.problem: You sell 10-class and 20-class packs, but your booking system can't change a pack once it's sold, your students can't see how many classes they have left, and you end up keeping a side spreadsheet. At month end you have no idea how many prepaid classes you still owe, so your bookkeeper either guesses or books it all as income on the day it was paid.
public.forWhom: Owners of small yoga, pilates, dance, pottery and fitness studios with one to five instructors who take card payments through a point-of-sale system and sell class packs.
benefits: No more side spreadsheet of who has classes left
Students see their own balance and get a reminder before credits expire
Fast name or QR check-in at the door
A month-end number for prepaid classes you still owe, ready for your bookkeeper
Keep the payment and booking setup you already have

ideas.problemStatement: Studios that run on Square sell prepaid packs through Square Appointments packages, which cannot be edited after creation, are capped at one-year expiry, do not show students their remaining credits, and give no report of unused credits. Owners say they 'manually keep track of students' (poster A), keep 'a separate spreadsheet every week' (poster B), and field 'Do I still have classes left?' questions (poster C). The bookkeeping side, prepaid classes as a liability released on attendance or at expiry, is standard practice in bookkeeping guides but no lightweight tool produces it for a Square studio.
ideas.description: The studio connects its Square account and marks which catalog items are packs. Square order webhooks credit the customer when one is bought and reverse on refund, and the balance is mirrored into a Square customer custom attribute so staff see it in Square too. At the door the owner checks students in by name or QR and one credit comes off the oldest-expiring eligible pack. A nightly job expires packs, emails students before credits lapse, and freezes a month-end snapshot. The month-end report shows packs sold, credits used and credits still owed; the bookkeeper export is built only if the validation test shows studios or their bookkeepers want it.
ideas.targetCustomer: Owner-operators of 1-to-5-instructor yoga, pilates, dance, pottery or fitness studios that take payments on Square, sell packs as plain Square items, and are not paying for Square Appointments Plus ($49/month, needed for Square's own packages) or Punchpass ($59/month).
ideas.buyer: The studio owner, from the business card, as a monthly software subscription; possibly recommended by the studio's bookkeeper.
ideas.whyNow: A Key West yoga studio owner asked Square on 2026-08-25 for packages that can be modified, saying they track students by hand (https://community.squareup.com/t5/Feature-Requests/Modify-Yoga-Packages/idi-p/848579), Square's help page still says pack contents and expiry cannot be edited, and October 2026 bookkeeping guides tell studios to treat prepaid packs as liabilities (https://catchingnumbers.com/blog/gym-fitness-studio-bookkeeping/).
ideas.founderFit: Yusuf Pisan can ship a web app alone in days on the HintWise platform, which already provides sign-in, per-app data, scheduled jobs, email and a small backend for the Square OAuth and webhook handling; the ledger rules are a well-bounded engine suited to an agent-built, test-driven build.

ideas.problemStatement: Small Shopify sellers who run scheduled pickup routes (meeting-point stops on set days) rebuild who-collects-what per stop by hand, and their date-picker apps sometimes let customers book closed days. A raw pet food seller running several routes cannot manage route orders cleanly in Shopify, and picker reviews describe closed-day bookings slipping through. Shopify's delivery method is read-only after checkout, so moving an order between pickup and shipping stays a native gap no app can close.
ideas.description: An embedded Shopify app that sits beside a free or cheap pickup date picker. The merchant defines routes and stops with weekly schedules, caps and skip dates; orders map to a route-day from the pickup location or from the date attribute Zapiet, Pickeasy or Genie writes. Each route-day produces a packing total and a per-stop manifest that the driver checks off on a phone, which marks orders picked up in Shopify. Scheduled jobs email customers the day before and when a stop is skipped, and a nightly audit flags orders on closed days, over a stop's cap or with no stop. It does not change Shopify's delivery method, which the Admin API does not allow.

ideas.problemStatement: On Fly.io, resources keep billing after you stop paying attention: stopped Machines are billed for their root filesystem, volumes are billed while detached, and a Managed Postgres cluster starts at $38 a month. Fly's docs say "We don't support billing alerts (yet), so budget accordingly", and there is no read-only endpoint for accrued cost, so solo developers learn about a forgotten 40-machine batch run or an unattached database from the invoice.
ideas.description: The team either runs a small self-hosted job that keeps its Fly token on its side and sends only resource metadata, or pastes an org-scoped read-only token (`fly tokens create readonly`), after being told that such a token can also read its databases. Each night the service lists apps, machines, volumes, Managed Postgres clusters and IPs through the Machines API, reads 7 days of per-app traffic from the org's Prometheus endpoint, and prices every resource from Fly's public regional price list. It flags likely waste (detached volumes, volumes on long-stopped machines, started machines with almost no traffic, clusters no app uses, machines beyond the declared count) with each item's monthly cost and the command to remove it. A digest email and a threshold alert on the projected month do the job Fly's dashboard does not. It is Fly.io only at launch; Render (no native spending limit) is the possible second provider, while Railway, Vercel and Supabase already have native limits and are out of scope.
ideas.targetCustomer: Two-to-ten-person startups and small agencies on paid Fly.io organizations with several apps, often with Managed Postgres, who check the dashboard rarely. Hobby personal orgs are left to Fly's new capped Free plan.
ideas.buyer: The founder or developer, on the personal or company card that already pays the Fly.io bill.
ideas.whyNow: Fly's cost-management doc still says it does not support billing alerts, and a 2026-11-10 forum request for 50/80/90% budget alerts was told it is not supported (https://community.fly.io/t/29045.json). Fly put Managed Postgres clusters on the Machines API on 2026-09-15 (https://fly.io/changelog/managed-postgres-machines-api.md), which makes the orphaned-database check possible. Fly's Free plan for personal orgs (launching 2026-11-23) caps hobby spend, which leaves paid team orgs as the uncovered buyer.
ideas.founderFit: Pisan can ship a web app alone in days on the HintWise platform, which already provides sign-in, per-app data, scheduled jobs and transactional email, the four parts this product needs. As a CS professor who teaches with agentic coding tools, he can also write the price model and waste rules as tested domain logic rather than a dashboard scrape.

ideas.techStack: Static React + Vite front end, Supabase auth and per-app tables (encrypted token, snapshots, flags), scheduled job and Fly Machines API plus Prometheus client on the Render backend, transactional email; no LLM needed.

pricing.rationale: Beside small-team spend monitors that do not cover Fly (Spendwall Pro $7, FreeTier Sentinel Pro $5); one unattached Basic Postgres cluster costs more than that each month. Free scripts and agent skills set a low ceiling.

ideas.revenueSketch: Estimate: 100 paying team orgs x $9/month = $900 MRR after a year; unproven, since nobody was found paying a third party for Fly cost monitoring.
ideas.distribution: First 10 customers from community.fly.io: post the free waste scan in the Show & Tell category, which exists for projects built on Fly (https://community.fly.io/categories.json); the forum guidelines forbid spam and ask members to avoid its appearance, with no explicit self-promotion rule (https://community.fly.io/faq.json), so reply in billing threads only where the scan answers the question. Then a Show HN post. The waste scan doubles as the lead magnet.

validationTest.method: A landing page describing the nightly watch and the self-hosted collector, shared in Fly's Show & Tell within the forum's rules, plus 5 interviews with teams on paid Fly orgs; offer a $9/month pre-order. Before building, test which endpoints a real read-only token reaches and whether a narrower token can be made that cannot query databases.
validationTest.successCriteria: Within 3 weeks: 8 pre-orders from paid team orgs, and at least 3 of 5 interviewed teams reporting a surprise bill in the last year.
validationTest.cost: About 2 days of work and $0 in ads.

ideas.moat: Thin. The value is a tested price model and waste rules kept current with Fly's price changes and API, plus history and trust with read-only tokens. Fly could ship billing alerts at any time, which would remove the threshold half but probably not the per-resource waste list.
compliance: Credential custody: Fly's Query Database endpoint 'can read every table' with only read access to the organization (https://docs.fly.io/api/machines/postgres-clusters/query-database.md), so a stored read-only org token exposes the customer's production data, including their end users' personal data. Offer the self-hosted collector by default, encrypt any stored token, never log it, and show how to revoke it.

GDPR: with the self-hosted collector the service holds only account emails and resource metadata (app and machine names); a privacy notice, a data processing addendum for EU customers, and deletion on cancel.
Accuracy: figures are estimates from the public price list, not invoices; label every number and disclaim liability for billing decisions.
Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 AA for the dashboard and HTML email.

risks.risk: Fly ships native billing alerts or caps; its docs say 'yet' and a forum reply mentions a docs branch with limited caps.
risks.mitigation: Lead with the per-resource waste list, which a total-spend alert does not give; keep the build small and watch Fly's changelog.

risks.risk: The read-only token may not cover Managed Postgres listing or Prometheus for every org (not verified this run).
risks.mitigation: Test with a real read-only token in milestone 1; fall back to an org deploy token only with explicit consent, or drop the check.

risks.risk: Estimates diverge from invoices after price changes (October 2026 CPU/RAM change) or regional pricing.
risks.mitigation: Versioned price table with a test per pricing-page example; show 'estimate' everywhere; let users report a mismatch.

risks.risk: Small market: only Fly.io customers who pay their own bill and check rarely.
risks.mitigation: Add Render as a second provider if the scan converts; Render's spending-limit request has 105 votes and no native limit.

risks.risk: Buyers prefer free: Accident Forgiveness refunds mistakes, Fly's Free plan caps hobby orgs, and free scripts and agent skills audit on demand.
risks.mitigation: Sell only the unattended part (nightly flags, history, threshold alert) to paid team orgs; drop the free scan.

risks.risk: Teams refuse to hand a third party a token that can read their databases.
risks.mitigation: Make the self-hosted collector the default path; look for a narrower attenuated token before launch.

scoreRationale.pain: Real complaints are fewer than seven. johngroot is building cost tooling (https://community.fly.io/t/28382.json), D. Voorhees built his own tool (http://dvoorhees.com/2026/08/06/fly-io-doesnt-have-a-daily-billing-endpoint-so-i-built-one/), the Sprites ask is out of scope (https://community.fly.io/t/29083.json) and the 10-04 post is about abuse. The three real money-loss posts are 95-108 days old, and a regular says refunds are 'nearly always' granted (https://community.fly.io/t/28402.json). That leaves one in-scope request inside 60 days (https://community.fly.io/t/29045.json), so 3.
scoreRationale.willingnessToPay: No payment evidence. The only builders made free tools (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/d-voorhees/flyio-usage-monitoring/main/CHANGELOG.md, https://tonsofskills.com/skills/flyio-cost-tuning/), and Fly's own engineer sends users who want limits to Railway (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48701567), so 2 stands.
scoreRationale.reachability: community.fly.io is open and billing threads recur (https://community.fly.io/t/29045.json), but no audience and anti-spam guidelines keep it at 3.
scoreRationale.competitiveGap: Fly's Free plan PR (#2661, 2026-11-17: '$5 of usage a month for personal orgs, launching 23 Nov', and it also edits the cost-management page) brings caps for hobby orgs. A free MIT agent skill already audits stopped Machines, unattached volumes, unused IPs and unreferenced databases on demand (https://tonsofskills.com/skills/flyio-cost-tuning/), and the free script gives daily compute estimates (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/d-voorhees/flyio-usage-monitoring/main/CHANGELOG.md). Only unattended nightly waste flags and threshold alerts for paid orgs remain open, so 3.
scoreRationale.feasibility: Endpoints now exist for every input: org-wide List All Machines, List All Volumes (attached_machine_id null when detached), List Postgres Clusters with attached_apps, and per-app IP assignments (https://docs.fly.io/llms.txt). A read-only token is proven on the Machines API and Prometheus (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/d-voorhees/flyio-usage-monitoring/main/CHANGELOG.md, v1.2). The read-only scope for clusters and IPs is still undocumented, so 4 stands.
scoreRationale.complianceBurden: Fly's Query Database endpoint 'can read every table' and 'Requires only read access to the organization' (https://docs.fly.io/api/machines/postgres-clusters/query-database.md). A stored read-only org token therefore exposes every customer's production database, including their end users' PII. The pitch 'read-only, so nothing can be changed' understates this, so 3.

review.findings: Fly's own billing work is imminent but narrow. Docs PR #2661 (Fly docs staff, opened 2026-11-17, draft) adds a Free plan with '$5 of usage a month for personal orgs, launching 23 Nov' and edits the cost-management page. A forum regular describes it as capped, with 'no possibility of surprise bills' (https://community.fly.io/t/29083.json). The changelog through 2026-11-12 shows no alerts or caps for paid orgs (https://fly.io/changelog), and the docs still say 'no billing alerts (yet)'. The free flyio-usage-monitoring script is not a full replacement: it covers compute only, uses one flat rate, and has had no update since 2026-08-12. A free MIT agent skill (flyio-cost-tuning) and Fly's new MCP do cover a one-time waste audit for free, so the draft's free scan has little value as a lead magnet. Fly's API docs now list org-wide machines, volumes (detached ones are detectable), Postgres clusters with attached_apps, and per-app IPs. Read-only scope is proven only for machines and Prometheus. The Query Database endpoint works with read-only org access, which makes custody of the token much more sensitive. Of the nine evidence items, two come from tool builders, two are off-scope (Sprites, abuse) and one is opinion. Fly reports more than 37,000 customers (https://fly.io/news/fly-io-launches-computers-for-agents.md), so 150 paying orgs is about 0.4%, but hobby personal orgs will move to the Free plan and cost-sensitive users are sent to Railway. Scores change: pain 4 to 3, competitiveGap 4 to 3, complianceBurden 4 to 3, total 21 to 18. Re-scoped on review to paid team orgs, the unattended nightly flags and threshold alert only, with a self-hosted collector so the token can stay with the customer; the free scan dropped; evidence from tool builders, off-scope posts and opinion removed.

missing: pain 3 is below 4 (after review, one in-scope request within 60 days; the money-loss posts are 95 to 108 days old and were refunded)
willingnessToPay 2 is below 3 (nobody found paying a third party for Fly cost monitoring)
gateGap.closedBy: The pre-order page in validationTest: 8 pre-orders from paid team orgs would lift willingnessToPay to 3 or 4, and three interviewed teams with a recent surprise bill would lift pain to 4, taking the total to 20 or more.

runNotes.caveats: First run of 2026-11-18 (Wednesday, developer and research tooling lens). Four provisional ideas ship, all at 18; none came near the gate of 22. Twenty-eight candidates were generated; nine were researched and adversarially reviewed, four survived (all rescored down 1 to 3 points) and five were killed: Harvest History Carry-Over (one-time migration; paid importers already carry invoices), Client API Sunset Desk (no matching complaint; apibreaks.com went unmaintained), Client Asset Register (InstaRenewal sells the same register), Retainer Month Note (free n8n and GitHub reporting tools) and Party Rental Run Sheet (misread evidence; free route apps). Reviewing stopped at nine because four had survived. The reviewers' main finding across the day: complaints that look strong are often vendors validating their own tools, or ask for something no add-on can deliver (Shopify's read-only delivery method, Calendly's own disconnection email). Selection constraints: two ideas are Small Business Ops and the other two carry smallBusiness true; every idea is substantial and Multi-week with a buildPlan; there is no Weekend MVP, because every Weekend-sized candidate (CSV preflight, TV menu, no-show rules) lacked complaint evidence and none was reviewed, so the Weekend MVP plus Multi-week constraint is not met. The Harvest price change (November 2026) is the strongest complaint cluster of the run but every product shape for it was already served. Fly.io launches a capped Free plan for personal orgs on 2026-11-23 (docs PR #2661), which the Idle Spend Watch scope already excludes. Square has paused new App Marketplace partnerships since September 2026, so Square add-ons cannot count on a store listing. Watchlist entries were all first seen today.
